chapters.title: Chapter 3: Sourcing Alternative Data: Vendors, Costs, and Compliance

lessons.title: Mapping the Alternative Data Vendor Landscape: Global and India-Specific

body.text: Finding a good dataset is a search process with defined steps, not a browsing session that ends when something looks impressive on a landing page.

children.text: Chapter 2 gave you the taxonomy of what exists. This chapter turns to the practical work of actually acquiring it: finding vendors, running a proper search process, pricing it correctly, staying compliant, and deciding what to build in-house. This lesson starts with the search itself, because most wasted budget in this field comes from licensing the first plausible-looking vendor a desk finds, rather than running a structured process across the full landscape.

body.title: Run This Before You Contact a Single Vendor
steps: Write down the exact hypothesis and feature you need, not a vague category like 'consumer data', but a specific claim such as 'retail footfall two weeks ahead of a quarterly result'
Search discovery platforms, relevant government portals, and academic literature for anything that could plausibly produce that feature
Build a shortlist of three to six candidates and request a trial or sample dataset from each, never rely on marketing slides alone
Score every trial sample on the six-dimension framework from Chapter 1, using the actual sample data, not the vendor's own claims about it
Only after scoring, move to commercial negotiation and vendor risk assessment, covered later in this chapter

children.text: Where to Actually Look: Discovery Channels

body.caption: No single channel covers the whole landscape, use at least three of these for any serious search

cells: Catalogued vendors searchable by sector, geography, and use case, such as Eagle Alpha and Neudata
Coverage is strongest for vendors who pay to be listed, so absence from these platforms does not mean a source doesn't exist
Sources like VAHAN, GSTN's e-way bill system, NPCI, MCA21, and data.gov.in, covered in Chapter 2
Free and legitimate, but usually requires you to build the pipeline yourself rather than buying a finished product
Researchers often name and cite the exact dataset or vendor they used to produce a published result
Academic access terms and pricing for commercial use can differ sharply from what a paper's authors paid or were granted
Informal referrals from analysts at other funds, quant meetups, and vendor conference floors
The most reliable source of honest, off-the-record feedback about a vendor's actual data quality and support

body.title: Two Different Pools, Two Different Risks

columns.label: Global Vendors Expanding Into India
points: Often stronger engineering, backfill discipline, and platform reliability, built for larger, more mature markets first
India coverage is frequently newer and thinner than their flagship US or European coverage
Pricing is usually set globally, which can make an India-only use case feel expensive relative to the India-specific value delivered
Marketing materials rarely distinguish clearly between global panel strength and India panel strength

columns.label: India-Specific and Homegrown Vendors
points: Built around Indian sources from the start, often with a better native understanding of local nuance, such as festival seasonality or Hinglish text
Typically newer companies, with a shorter track record and less proven operational resilience
Pricing tends to be more negotiable and closer to the actual value of a narrower, India-only product
Fewer competitors in most sub-categories, which can mean less pressure on them to keep improving data quality

children.text: Neither pool is automatically the right choice. The mistake to avoid is assuming a global vendor's brand recognition guarantees India data quality, when the honest answer is that you do not know until you have actually seen an India-specific trial sample.

body.title: Evaluating a '50 Countries Including India' Pitch
body.scenario: A well known global web-traffic analytics vendor pitches your desk on its coverage of 50 countries, including India, with impressive case studies from its US and European clients. The sales deck shows aggregate global metrics but no India-specific detail.
body.prompt: Before agreeing to a paid pilot, what should you specifically demand from this vendor, and why does their strong global reputation not settle the question?
body.modelAnswer: A strong global reputation says nothing about the size of the underlying panel the vendor uses to estimate Indian website traffic specifically, and a small India panel can produce noisy, unreliable estimates even from an otherwise excellent company, exactly the estimation risk covered in Chapter 2's lesson on web and app data. Before agreeing to anything paid, demand an India-only trial sample covering at least a handful of well known Indian websites or apps whose real traffic or user base you can sanity check against independent public information, ask directly what share of their global panel is India-based, and request the estimate's stated confidence interval or error range for India specifically rather than accepting a single global methodology description. If the vendor cannot or will not provide India-specific validation data, that refusal is itself informative, and the correct next step is to treat this as unproven for India until shown otherwise, regardless of how strong their US or European case studies look.

children.text: Vendor Longevity Risk: The Dependency You Don't Price In

A dataset that scores well on all six dimensions can still be a bad long-term bet if the company producing it is small, poorly funded, or dependent on a single unstable data-sharing agreement of its own. If a live strategy depends on a feed that vendor discontinues, gets acquired and repriced, or simply lets degrade, you inherit that risk the moment the strategy goes live, and it rarely shows up until the worst possible time, mid-position, with no fallback ready.

stats.label: Contractual protection
stats.context: Negotiate a minimum advance notice period before a vendor can discontinue or materially change a feed you depend on

stats.label: Continuity planning
stats.context: For critical feeds, negotiate access to historical data or documented methodology if the vendor ceases operations

stats.label: The real fallback
stats.context: Knowing roughly how you would rebuild the feed yourself, covered in this chapter's build-vs-buy lesson, is the only fallback you fully control

body.text: Every vendor evaluation has two separate questions hiding inside it: is this data good, and is this company going to still exist and still support this product in three years. Desks that only ask the first question get surprised by the second one at the worst time.

Vendor and platform names mentioned in this lesson illustrate categories of business models for education only and are not endorsements. Always run your own due diligence, trial period, and legal review before entering any commercial data agreement.

points: Run a structured five-step search, define the hypothesis, search discovery channels, shortlist and trial, score on six dimensions, then negotiate, rather than licensing the first plausible vendor
Use at least three discovery channels: evaluation platforms, government portals, academic literature, and peer or conference networks, since no single channel covers the full landscape
Global vendors expanding into India often bring stronger engineering but thinner India-specific panels, while India-specific vendors understand local nuance but carry more track-record risk
A vendor's global reputation does not validate its India data quality, always demand an India-specific trial sample with some form of independent sanity check
Vendor longevity is a real, underpriced risk: a good dataset from a fragile company can leave a live strategy without its key input with little warning
Protect against longevity risk with contractual notice periods, data or methodology escrow for critical feeds, and a realistic sense of your own ability to rebuild the feed in-house if needed
